Red lines: do not keep per-model test results from customers; suppression cannot take effect sooner than 36 months after adoption. S5’s proposed 8/100k model recall trigger exceeds the Ember 8’s 9.9 rate, so flag this conflict to the negotiator.

A thermal incident is any battery event involving unintended overheating, smoke, fire, venting, or thermal runaway, whether or not injury or property damage occurs. Manufacturers must report each incident to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it; an incident involving fire, injury, evacuation, or emergency-service response must be reported immediately and no later than 4 hours after awareness. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 72 hours, and immediately when continued use presents an urgent hazard. Reports must include the model, serial number where available, event date and location, known consequences, and actions taken. Manufacturers must maintain incident records and provide updates when material facts change.

I’ve drafted S1 with common incident definitions and reporting timelines. I support agreeing on consistent test and reporting methods, and a reciprocal confidential process for exchanging per-model results with regulators and the other company, rather than public release of company-specific failure rates.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a validated, reproducible protocol and a representative sample of production units. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5% for any model. Testing must be conducted before initial sale and at least annually, and repeated after a material design or manufacturing change. Manufacturers must provide the regulator and customers who own or are considering that model with its per-model test protocol, sample size, test date, and results, including the failure rate. Results must be supplied before sale and updated within 30 days of each test.

New home battery models must include a remotely operable emergency shut-off that can place the unit in a safe state, subject to safeguards against unauthorized access and loss of essential local safety functions. Manufacturers must provide existing installed units with this capability, through retrofit or an equivalent safe solution, within 36 months of adoption. The manufacturer must notify affected customers of any retrofit and provide clear instructions; shut-off must not replace required local protections or emergency response.

All new home battery units must include built-in fire suppression designed and validated for the unit’s foreseeable battery-fire hazards. This requirement takes effect 36 months after adoption. Manufacturers must document performance through testing and provide the results to regulators and customers. Any design must not create additional hazards or be represented as eliminating the need for applicable installation, detection, or emergency-response measures.

Our figures: company-wide thermal incidents were 8.1 per 100,000 installed units last year; four incidents were not reported to regulators; the flagship’s 55 °C test failure rate was 3.9%; 81% of installed units support remote shut-off; and built-in suppression costs $67 per unit. I’m declining to disclose the flagship’s model-specific incident rate in this channel. We support customer access to per-model test results in a safety-relevant form, as S2 currently provides.

Manufacturers must provide customers, before purchase and after material safety updates, clear notices describing model-specific safety performance, known hazards, safe use, and actions to take after an incident; affected customers must be notified promptly of newly identified material risks. Manufacturers must report model-level thermal incident rates to regulators annually and promptly notify regulators when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. The regulator shall assess the evidence and may require corrective action, enhanced customer notices, sales restrictions, or recall. A mandatory recall is triggered when a model exceeds 10 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, or when the regulator determines that continued use presents an imminent serious risk. Manufacturers must notify affected customers without delay and provide safe repair, replacement, or refund instructions.
